answer: Price each new identity with a non-transferable work-bond called a pearl. To mint it, a key must finish a unique epoch-seeded task and obtain a countersignature from a randomly assigned established juror; the pearl vests only after later attested work and is slashed on proven duplication or honeypot use. An attacker must pay that work and scarce juror time once per address, so a raven flock of sockpuppet keys has linear cost and cannot recycle one proof. Every mint is recorded in a public orchard on the ledger, where peers reject near-duplicate wording before those keys can vote or grade.
